passage: On Diwali evening Kamal scrolled past a photo of the family's rooftop puja in Hyderabad: everyone lined up, and a gap at the end. It was the third festival without an invitation. Kamal set the phone on the sofa, and a hollow ache spread through the chest. No anger tonight, only the flat sadness of a chair nobody moves. The doorbell rang. Rukmini stood there with a box of sweets and two friends from the office, saying, "We have too much halwa. Save us." Kamal laughed, then cried a little into the kitchen towel. Later, over cards, Kamal said, "I am not going to argue about who was right anymore." Rukmini nodded and dealt again.

qa.q: What did Rukmini bring to the door?
qa.a: Rukmini brought a box of sweets and two friends from the office.

qa.q: What was Kamal feeling on seeing the photo of the rooftop puja?
qa.a: A hollow ache of grief over the lost bond, rather than anger.

qa.q: How is Kamal building a chosen family?
qa.a: By opening the door to Rukmini and the friends, sharing food and cards and letting the sadness show.

qa.q: How might Rukmini see Kamal's tears?
qa.a: Rukmini seems to accept them without fuss, nodding and dealing the next hand, giving Kamal room to feel them.

grounding: Family gatherings go on without the protagonist, who mourns the lost bond, leans on chosen family and stops needing to win the story.

passage:
Diwali, the first year: Harish scrolled through his cousin's photos from the family house, everyone on the terrace with diyas, and no chair for him in any picture. He switched off the phone and sat in the dark flat, chest hollow.
A Tuesday in March: Rashmi from the office found him staring at his thali at lunch. He told her, haltingly, that his parents still did not speak to him since he married outside the community. Rashmi did not argue about who was right. "Come to ours for Holi," she said.
The next Diwali: eight friends crowded his small balcony with borrowed lamps. Harish still checked the family photos once, felt the old ache, and let it be. Then he went back out, lit the last diya, and did not post anything to prove a point.

qa.q: What did Rashmi invite Harish to?
qa.a: To come to theirs for Holi.

qa.q: How does Harish feel on the first Diwali, and what shows it?
qa.a: He feels a hollow grief and loneliness; he switches off the phone and sits in the dark after seeing family photos with no place for him.

qa.q: How does Harish handle the ache by the next Diwali?
qa.a: He lets himself feel it, looks at the photos once, then returns to his friends and does not post anything to prove who was right.

qa.q: How might Rashmi see Harish when she finds him staring at his thali?
qa.a: She sees a friend quietly hurting and chooses to offer company for Holi instead of taking sides in his family story.

grounding: The protagonist mourns being left out of family gatherings, builds a circle of friends, and stops needing to prove who was right.

passage: You asked why I never go to the Jabalpur weddings, Saurabh. Sit. When I was a young woman of twenty-five, my brothers and I fought over whether I would marry the man I had chosen. After that, the invitations simply stopped. I would hear about a naming ceremony a month later, from a neighbour. That first year I cried in the bathroom so your grandfather wouldn't see. Then Kamala-akka, who taught with me at the girls' school, started taking me to her family's festivals. Her mother saved me a seat at every puja. Slowly I had people again. I also stopped writing long letters explaining my side. I kept my manners, sent a card when someone passed away, and let them think what they liked. That is how your Manjula-paati learned to live well without winning the argument.

qa.q: What happened to the invitations after the fight with Manjula's brothers?
qa.a: They simply stopped, and Manjula heard about a naming ceremony a month later from a neighbour.

qa.q: What was Manjula feeling that first year, and how do we know?
qa.a: She felt grief and loneliness at being cut off; she cried in the bathroom so her husband would not see.

qa.q: What turning point in the story helped Manjula build a new circle?
qa.a: Accepting Kamala-akka's invitations to her family's festivals gave Manjula people to belong with, and she stopped writing long letters defending her side.

qa.q: How might Kamala-akka's mother have seen the young Manjula?
qa.a: She probably saw a lonely young teacher from her daughter's school and wanted her to feel welcome, so she saved her a seat at every puja.

grounding: An elder recalls mourning exclusion from family events, finding a chosen circle of friends, and keeping her values without arguing her case.
